SACRED CONFLICT

By: Matuba Mahlatjie | Commission

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
As South Africa grapples with the tension between Christian theology and African ancestral beliefs, we investigate the Catholic Church’s radical new school policy for children experiencing

Unique Selling Point:
For centuries, a spiritual war raged on South African soil. Christianity called traditional beliefs ‘pagan.’ Ancestral veneration was branded ‘devil worship.’ Today, that battle echoes in our classrooms… where children hear voices science can’t explain.

Summary:
South Africa’s Catholic schools have quietly launched a first-of-its-kind policy (January 2024) to support learners claiming ancestral callings to become sangomas. This guideline, balancing child safety, cultural respect, and Catholic doctrine, ignites a deeper conflict: Is praying to ancestors worship or veneration? Can Christianity and African spirituality ever reconcile?

Script:



(Govan) These prayers are not witchcraft. They are not superstition. These are sangomas sending prayers to their ancestors.



(Govan) To be a sangoma, some are called young while others experience the calling later in life.



(Precious Ntloko) The signs started when she was three years old. She had eczema. The whole body started peeling off. She started scratching. We continued with her treatment up until they couldn't treat it anymore on her skin. Then another sign that showed that she has an ancestral calling…



(Precious Ntloko Subtitles) ...she had constant, vivid dreams.



(Govan) That was 11 years ago. Buhle is now 14. Her mother, Precious Ntloko, says, like her, Buhle has been chosen. The skin rashes, dreams and difficulties socialising with other children.



(Govan) Clear signs of her calling as a spiritual healer.



(Precious Ntloko) I used to be ignorant of that because I didn't think that I would have a child so young being exposed to ubungoma as a whole, and also being a young sangoma.



(Govan) Becoming a sangoma is a calling. Known in isiZulu as “ubungoma”, it’s considered a gift from the ancestors, a destiny to serve and heal the community.



(Precious Ntloko) Being a sangoma, it's not witchcraft. It's a way of healing; it’s a natural way of healing that it's passed through your ancestors to you. As a sangoma, you're a counsellor, you understand. You must mentor. You are a leader in the community.



(Govan) But in our modern world, Buhle represents a dilemma: how to cater for children like her in a society and schooling system suspicious of traditional beliefs.



(Precious Ntloko) In the community that we live in, the stigma around it… You wouldn't want to expose your child with that because it comes with lot of negativity when you are a sangoma.



(Govan) Children like Buhle are caught in conflicting worlds; a sacred calling tied to African spirituality and systemic neglect at school.



(Govan) Sangomas play a pivotal role in the lives of around 15 million South Africans. It’s a position steeped in rituals and responsibilities usually associated with adults. But every now and then, it’s believed the ancestors call on children to embark on this journey.



(Priest Thulani Skhosana) To be honest, we are aware that the church has not really fully taken root in the life of Africans. They have always lived a double life. I must say, they have never really abandoned their cultures.



(Govan) Father Thulani Skhosana is a Catholic priest. His church has developed a new policy aimed at bridging the divide between established Western religion and traditional beliefs in Catholic schools. It’s the first time it’s being attempted.



(Priest Thulani Skhosana) Anyone who is a sangoma is welcome in the Catholic church right now.



(Govan) But that might change.



(Priest Thulani Skhosana) Yeah, it may change. Not in a way of you may be expelled. Maybe there may be a question of, in this ubungoma, let's see, can this be compatible with the Catholic church?



(Govan) In 2024, the National Catholic Board of Education issued policy guidelines for all Catholic schools nationwide in a bid to safeguard well-being of children experiencing ancestral callings. The guidelines call on schools to collaborate with families without any spiritual intervention.



(Priest Thulani Skhosana) A child is not going to be expelled because they've manifested the signs. A child is not going to be demonised, is not going to be segregated. It's not a theological position. It is a recognition. And that position, though, is in line with the present position of the church which respects all religions and accepts that there is an element of good in every religion.



(Govan) Under the policy, Catholic schools will try to protect children like Buhle. But the church is adamant it’s a practical solution rather than an endorsement of the practice.



(Priest Thulani Skhosana) The church is not teaching that this is accepted in the church. When you become a sangoma, you are called. So, it's a lifelong commitment and surrender, and understanding this – that ubungoma is a calling. When you become a sangoma, you don't, as a sangoma, own ubungoma. It is the ancestors who gave you ubungoma, who owned that ubungoma. So, you owe them obedience and respect.



(Govan) Father Thulani says being a sangoma presents theological challenges, in essence coming down to whether obedience is owed to Jesus or the ancestors.



(Priest Thulani Skhosana) So, the radical question then comes from Matthew chapter six, that you cannot serve both masters.



(Precious Ntloko) They go hand in hand. It goes through spirituality as a whole. What makes you calmer, what makes you… What do you believe in? I believe in God, but I also acknowledge my ancestors. They wanted me to embark on this journey, and I did exactly that.



(Govan) Would you describe it as the marriage between your African spirituality and Christianity? Does it conflict, or do they fit each other?



(Precious Ntloko Subtitles) If Ubungoma is used in its purest form, they align.



(Govan) It’s a dilemma not likely to be resolved anytime soon. So, what happens to children like Buhle in the interim? Precious says her daughter was victimised and called a witch.



(Precious Ntloko) It was not nice at all. I've been to school, Yoh, a lot of times this year, I think fifth time since January, attending to the issue of bullying. Tomorrow, it's this story. But you could see it's around her being a healer. Until one teacher, the last meeting we had, we agreed that she's going to change schools.



(Govan) At the heart of the name-calling is “ubungoma”, a calling from the ancestors that Buhle’s classmates wouldn’t necessarily understand.



(Precious Ntloko) Most of the learners at school, they'll call her names that she has a snakeskin, that she didn't bath. Remember eczema, it makes you scratch. Then she'll feel like something is moving on her body, especially on her back. She would hear sounds, and then she would be sleepy, agitated.



(Priest Thulani Skhosana) We know we are coming from apartheid, colonialism, and where people who were sangomas were demonised. Some of them have been killed, accused of being witches. So, I think it is time for the church to be clear so that people don't have to live a double life.



(Govan) Historically, the church often responded to traditional beliefs and customs with brutality. People claiming to be called by their ancestors were treated with suspicion, accused of being demonic, evil and possessed. It’s why the church’s school policy draws a clear line: no exorcisms.



(Priest Thulani Skhosana) The policy has made it clear that genuine ancestral calling don't need exorcism. So, the first thing is we have to establish that it is genuine.



(Govan) But under the policy, it’ll be the church that decides which callings are authentic and which should be treated otherwise.



(Priest Thulani Skhosana) Now, as to how that is done, is another thing. But can there be context or situations where somebody is possessed by demonic forces that need prayer? Yes, they can be. So, the main thing is to make a discernment.



(Govan) Who makes the discernment?



(Priest Thulani Skhosana) Yeah, at the moment, it will be somebody who would know with regard to exorcism. We do have exorcists, people who are specialised with regard to demonic possession. So, if that person is called, they may be able to tell that this is a demonic possession, or they may be able to tell to say, “This is not demonic, but I don't know what it is.”



(Govan) It seems some old habits die hard. But creating a space where orthodox faith and indigenous beliefs can coexist was never going to be easy. The new policy is a step in the right direction in ensuring children like Buhle are protected… and respected.



(Precious Ntloko) How about we teach...



(Govan) Exactly.



(Precious Ntloko) … educate these learners about who's a sangoma, a prophet, a Hindu, and all these things. Let's teach even the parents to teach their kids that you don't have to be mean.
